title: Slide rules multiply by adding lengths, and one flew to the Moon on Apollo 11

cover.alt: Close-up of a Keuffel & Esser slide rule's finely engraved logarithmic scales, seen through its glass cursor.

body: A slide rule's scales are spaced by **logarithms**, and the logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms: log(x × y) = log x + log y. So sliding one scale along another adds two lengths, and the number you read off is the product. William Oughtred combined two of Edmund Gunter's logarithmic rules into a recognisable slide rule around 1622, shortly after John Napier published the idea of logarithms. For roughly three and a half centuries it was the everyday calculating tool of science and engineering, accurate to about three significant figures, until cheap pocket calculators made it obsolete in the mid-1970s.

slides.alt: Buzz Aldrin in a spacesuit inside the dark, cramped Gemini capsule, with a pipe in his mouth and a slide rule floating near him.
slides.caption: Buzz Aldrin on the Gemini 12 mission, with a slide rule floating beside him. Pickett aluminium slide rules flew on Apollo too, including Aldrin's own to the Moon.

slides.heading: Try 2 × 3
slides.text: Slide the 1 on the moving scale until it sits over 2 on the fixed scale. Then look along the moving scale to 3: the number underneath it on the fixed scale is 6. You have added the length for log 2 to the length for log 3.

steps.label: Each scale is marked at logarithmic spacing
Sliding adds the length of log x to log y
The scale at that point reads x × y

slides.question: The HP-35 of 1972 was the first handheld scientific calculator. What did it cost, in US dollars of the day?
slides.explanation: $395: fine for some engineers, too much for most students. By 1976 the TI-30 sold for under $25, and the slide rule's days were over.

slides.heading: Still in some cockpits
slides.text: One slide rule is still in daily use around the world: the E6-B, a circular slide rule made in the 1930s to help pilots with dead reckoning. Many sailors also keep a slide rule as a backup for navigation in case the electrics or batteries fail.

slides.question: A slide rule shows 6 for 2 × 3, and also for 20 × 30. How do you tell which answer is which?
options: You track the decimal point yourself
Use the back of the rule
slides.explanation: The rule only gives the digits. Users kept track of the decimal point in their heads or with scientific notation, which made them less likely to trust false precision.
